pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words, citing their own NOTES.md numbers wherever the question asks for evidence; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Describe the optimization loop you followed, step by step. Why is optimizing without a profile called malpractice rather than just wasteful?
expected_points: measure a baseline, hypothesize (written down before editing), make the smallest change, re-measure with the same benchmark
no measured improvement means revert — the complexity is not paid for
correctness tests must still pass; an optimization that changes behavior is a bug
intuition about where time goes is reliably wrong, so guessing pays real costs (readability, risk, time) for unverified benefit
the profile turns 'I think the loop is slow' into 'this line is 84% of samples'

questions.prompt: What makes a benchmark meaningful rather than a random number? Cover b.N, b.ReportAllocs, the sink variable, sub-benchmarks, and why you ran benchstat instead of reading one run.
expected_points: the framework grows b.N until the run is long enough for a stable ns/op, so the loop body must do identical work every iteration; b.ResetTimer keeps setup out of the measurement
b.ReportAllocs adds allocs/op and B/op — the GC-pressure currency, often a better production predictor than ns/op
assigning the result to a package-level sink stops dead-code elimination from deleting the work being measured
b.Run sweeps input sizes: watching ns/op as n grows 10x exposes super-linear behavior (their Render sweep grows ~200x for 20x input)
single runs move 5-20% with machine noise, so -count=10 plus benchstat; p=0.000 means the difference is real, '~' means no measured change
benchmarks and profiles run WITHOUT -race, which distorts every number 2-20x

questions.prompt: Walk me through reading your CPU profile: what do flat and cum mean, what does each combination tell you to do, and what did -list and the flame graph add that -top could not?
expected_points: flat = time in the function's own code; cum = the function plus everything it called
high flat means fix it here; high cum with low flat means the cost is downstream, follow the call
runtime.mallocgc / growslice / GC workers near the top means 'you allocate too much — go read the heap profile'
-list annotates the function's source line by line, turning the theory into a per-line number
flame graph: width = share of samples, stacking = call depth; read widths to tell 'one callee dominates' from 'death by a thousand cuts'
the CPU profiler samples ~100 times/second, so costs are statistical and a short run is mostly noise

questions.prompt: For each of TopUsers and Render: what did the profile blame, what did you change, and what did the measurement do? Why do the graded tests assert allocation counts instead of elapsed time?
expected_points: TopUsers: strings.ToLower ran once per comparison inside the linear scan — O(entries x users) calls, each allocating an escaping string; a map index plus lowering once per entry took ~508,000 allocations to ~10,000

Render: += builds a new, longer string per line (O(n) allocations, O(n^2) bytes copied — ~81 MB for 98 KB of output) and fmt.Sprintf boxes every argument; a sized strings.Builder plus strconv.AppendInt into a reused buffer took it to one allocation
cites their own benchstat rows with p-values, not just the lesson's numbers
allocation counts are deterministic under the race detector's 2-20x slowdown and under machine noise, so they are a fair automated gate
an allocation count also points at a specific mistake, whereas a slower number only says 'something is wrong'

questions.prompt: You mounted net/http/pprof in NewDebugMux. What does each profile type (cpu, heap, goroutine, block, mutex) answer, and how should these endpoints be exposed in production?
expected_points: profile = CPU: where the CPU goes, sampled for ?seconds=N
heap: who allocates (alloc_space/alloc_objects) or who holds memory right now (inuse_space)
goroutine: every goroutine's stack — the deadlock and goroutine-leak tool
block: where goroutines wait on channels/locks, off until runtime.SetBlockProfileRate; mutex: who holds contended locks, off until runtime.SetMutexProfileFraction
pprof.Index owns the /debug/pprof/ subtree and serves the named runtime profiles; cmdline, profile, symbol and trace are separate exact patterns that win over the subtree under the 1.22 mux rules
serve them on a private/internal port, never the public mux — a heap dump is an information disclosure; but leave them enabled, the profile captured during the incident is worth ten postmortems

questions.prompt: Memory in a running service climbs steadily over hours. Which profile and which sample index do you reach for, and how would that differ from diagnosing GC pressure?
expected_points: a leak/retention question is inuse_space (or inuse_objects): who is holding memory right now
GC pressure is alloc_space/alloc_objects: who is generating garbage, even if it dies immediately
picking the wrong index is the classic heap-profile mistake — this exercise's garbage is already collected, so inuse_space shows almost nothing
connects back to the GC lesson: allocation rate drives pacing, live set drives mark cost
compare two heap profiles over time, and check goroutine count too — a goroutine leak is also a memory leak

questions.prompt: The append-style Render is faster but longer and fussier than the fmt.Sprintf version. When would you reject that rewrite in review, and what would you need to see to approve it?
expected_points: off the hot path, fmt.Sprintf / fmt.Fprintf is good Go — readability wins by default
approve it when a profile names the line and a benchstat comparison shows a significant win on a workload that matters
the cost side is real: more code, more places to get formatting wrong, so correctness tests (byte-identical output) are part of the price
the general rule: reach for append-style, pooling or preallocation because the measurement said so, never as a default style
